mechanisms.statement: Per-problem solve probability is bimodal: each model has a block of problems it essentially never solves (base 33 of 500 at 0/4, 79 of 328 with no right sample) and a block it solves most of the time. A plurality vote only converts problems in the narrow middle band, so vote curves plateau within a few samples at the solvable fraction; a model that abstains (cap hits) instead of answering wrong has a vote close to pass@k.

holds_against.why: Agreeing wrong groups behind 43 % of vote failures are the low-p side of the middle band; they cap the plateau rather than letting it keep rising.
Think-SFT's MATH-500 vote beat one-axis forecasts because its errors are abstentions, so its vote approaches pass@4, which is this mechanism's claim.

mechanisms.statement: Each problem needs a derivation of a certain length. A cap hit is a cut answer, and raising the cap or adding finishing directions helps only where the cut text is an unfinished correct derivation (Think-SFT: about a quarter finish right). The base's and RL's cut answers are stalled, so finishing them yields guesses (base 4 of 64). So the payoff of more budget or more finishing scales with how many cut answers hold real long derivations.

holds_against.why: RL fixes the base's cap-hit problems at the matched-difficulty rate; on these sets needed length and difficulty are the same axis, so no separate stop policy is implied.
Forcing the base to commit at 8k loses problems: its long answers are stalled, not near the end of a derivation, as the mechanism says.

mechanisms.statement: Easy problems need short derivations, and on them a model answers in a short register. At T 1.0 the plain prompt's terse register derails on these short problems (plain base loses 28 points on short quartiles, none on the longest), while the deliberative register survives. Edits or prompts that install deliberation lengthen short answers on easy problems; the leftover short answers are mostly right, and the residual quick wrong answers sit on problems the cued base usually solves.

holds_against.why: A third of Think-SFT's easy-problem errors are cap hits, but two thirds are finished answers, so the easy side still fails mainly in finished short work.

mechanisms.statement: RL fixes problems in order of the length of the derivation they need. The first 100 steps install the deliberative opening and cut per-step slips, which pays on short and medium problems (step-100 finished answers +4.6 points). Finishing long derivations under the cap is learned only after step 400. So early checkpoints sit near the cued base on long, hard problems and gain mainly on short ones, and the cue adds little to a checkpoint that already opens this way.

holds_against.why: Step 100 is no sharper per token than the cued base; the slip cut comes from deliberating, not lower entropy, and needs no sharpening.

mechanisms.statement: Competition problems (AIME, HMMT; most of hard328, all of fresh2026) are limited by finding a working plan, not by executing steps: the base's errors on problems it never solves are wrong plans, and RL's finished wrong answers are 67 % wrong plans. RL weights and their top directions add finishing and fewer slips but no plans, so on contest sets they track RL; only imitation of long expert traces supplies plans, visible as high precision of finished long answers.

mechanisms.statement: The best size of a finishing edit depends on how many cut answers are on problems the model cannot solve. Raising the dose turns cut answers into finished ones: on solvable problems these are right, on unsolvable ones they are guesses that replace an abstention and, under a vote, outvote right samples. So the optimum dose is lower and the fall past it steeper on harder sets, while easy sets (MATH-500, code) show a flat top.
